In addition to this problem, I need to be able to display multiple lines of equations. The users I am working with will be using multiple sets of data and, because of this, they will need to have each line's regression equation. 


Is it possible to do this? I apologize if this is a very stupid question. I am not very great at math since I am an avid code monkey. 


As a side note, would the regression equations for the lm, glm, gam, loess, rlm be the same ? I am assuming they are not but I am only finding solutions dealing with the lm equation. 



Thanks so much for your help and time!



Amber James

messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Re: Equation Text for Multiple Regression Lines
parts:
Amber:

Now that Brandon has dragged my name into this ;D, the essential
problem is that your data analysts apparently believe that ggplot2 is
a somewhat self-contained statistical analysis and graphics system,
but it's not. The stat_smooth() function can fit models to the (x, y)
pairs it is given, but it does not retain the fitted model equation(s)
- it only returns x's and predicted values, as that is what is needed
for geom_smooth().

Each layer in a ggplot takes a data frame as input, but *you* have to
supply the data frame - ggplot2 does not generate one for you from the
output of a stat function. Consequently, ggplot2 is unable to deliver
the information you need to render a model equation as a text element
- it was not designed with that purpose in mind. To get what you want,
you have to fit the model(s) beforehand, extract the coefficients and
assemble a (list of) text string(s) that represent[s] the model
fit(s).

You can use the original data frame to generate scatterplot fits with
geom_smooth() given a model type. For the model equations, you could
create a separate data frame with (x, y) positions where the equations
are to be placed and a text string for the fitted model(s) in R's
plotmath notation.

Another problem is that some smoothers (such as loess) do not return a
fitted model equation and although GAMs do return one, they are linear
combinations of smoothers, so this complicates the way a text string
is constructed to represent the model fit.

Here's a reproducible example that compares a linear model with a
robust linear model using one of the data sets in Anscombe's quartet,
where the robust fit is tangibly different:

DF <- anscombe[, c("x3", "y3")]

# Fit the two models to the data
m1 <- lm(y3 ~ x3, data = DF)
m2 <- MASS::rlm(y3 ~ x3, data = DF)

# coef(m1); coef(m2) # extracts the fitted intercepts and slopes

# I fit the strings manually, but you could substitute
# the coefficient indices in the appropriate places
txtDF <- data.frame(x = 11.5, y = c(7, 10),
fit = c("hat(y) == 4 + 0.346~x", "hat(y)
== 3 + 0.5~x"))

ggplot(DF, aes(x = x3, y = y3)) +
geom_point() +
geom_smooth(method = lm, size = 1, se = FALSE) +
geom_smooth(method = MASS::rlm, size = 1, color = "darkorange", se = FALSE) +
geom_text(data = txtDF, aes(x = x, y = y, label = fit),
parse = TRUE, size = 5)

The argument parse = TRUE in geom_text() takes the input strings from
txtDF$fit and parses them using plotmath.

For something truly automated, you'd need to program the contents of
txtDF, including the x/y positions for the fitted model equations, but
this illustrates the general idea.

I imagine the Shiny app is ideated somewhat as follows:

* select the x/y variables, and/or the data frame, via select menus or
input boxes
* select one or more model types from a menu
* draw the graph with the selected model fits
* add the fitted equations as annotation

If this is the basic idea, your server.R script is likely to be pretty
extensive. I would expect you'd need to

* fit each selected model
* extract the coefficients
* build a text string that represents the fitted equation
* generate the data frame for the text strings
* generate the ggplot and add the parsed model fit strings

I would expect that you'd have to write separate code to accommodate
each of the supported models; moreover, you'd have to find a way to
programmatically set up where the model equations are going to be
placed.

You may want to look into ggvis as an alternative, as it supports a
wider range of models than does ggplot2 - it will accept almost any
modeling function with a predict() method if you use
layer_model_predictions() to generate the fits as a data
transformation. It's more of a work in progress than ggplot2 but it
works well with Shiny - in particular, it supports reactives. I'll
leave it as homework to check whether ggvis supports annotation - use
the development version on GitHub to check because it has the most
recently added features.

HTH,
Dennis

parts:
Just as an update I was able to get my program working exactly the way I needed it to. Thanks for the advice.  I adjusted the code from the ggplot_smooth_func.R file. 

I changed this line of code from the file


data.frame(x=min(data$x)*0.9, y=max(data$y)*0.9, label=func_string)


To this!
    gX <-data$minX -  (data$minX  *0.9)
    difY<- data$maxY-data$minY
    gY <-difY - (difY *.9)

    data.frame(x= data$minX - gX, y= (data$minY- (gY*data$gNum)), label=func_string)

The minX and maxX were added to the data frame. They are the absolute min and max of the entire set of data being plotted.  The gNum is also the numerical of the factored groups I am applying to the data set.  
So before making my ggPlot I add this to the data set. 

    dataToPlot$minX <- min(as.numeric(as.character( dataToPlot$xPlot )), na.rm=T)
    dataToPlot$maxY <- max(as.numeric(as.character( dataToPlot$yPlot )), na.rm=T)
    dataToPlot$minY <- min(as.numeric(as.character( dataToPlot$yPlot )), na.rm=T)
    dataToPlot$groupNum<- as.numeric(factor(dataToPlot$group))


My final call looks like : 

 ggplot(dataToPlot, aes(y = yPlot, x = xPlot, group = group,
               minX = minX,   minY = minY, maxY = maxY, gNum= groupNum,
               color = factor(group), fill = factor(group)))+
           stat_smooth(method= "lm", se=FALSE)

This is the resultant graph. Grouping were added to this for visual understanding of why we need the above code.


These changes allow for any number of groupings or data sizes. The result will always put the equation text in the lower part of the graph with all of the grouped equations evenly spaced. I realize that the given image has that silly square in it still. I am still not sure why this reappeared again. I ensured my Cairo package was updated but it did not fix the problem completely apparently. 


ANYWHO, thanks for the help. I hope that my solution helps some other people who faced the same issues that I did. 


Thanks, 


Amber James
